Dont blame lactic acid for sore muscles

"Adenine Triphosphate" is not a chemical. It's "Adenosine Triphosphate". I don't want to sit here and armchair-biologist this article too much, but I have to say that the evidence as presented here in this article is not enough to explain anything helpful.

In particular, the only mechanism discussed here is that 'calcium concentrations correlate directly with the strength of muscular response to nerve impulses' and then also 'creatine phosphate metabolism produces excess phosphate, which inhibits calcium build-up'. So, according to this article's presentation, that would mean that metabolising creatine preferentially over other kinds of metabolism would cause your muscles to become weak and stiff faster.

Only, this is the opposite of what happens. I stack creatine monohydrate so that when I go to work out, I have a stronger, longer-running workout. I can lift whole percentage points more when I'm stacked than I can when I let my creatine stores get exhausted. Moreover, when I'm stuffing my body with as much creatine monohydrate as I can manage, I recover much faster from my workouts, and I experience notably less stiffness and soreness. This is not just some quack anecdote, you can go out and try this for yourself. You can get pure creatine monohydrate--not part of some kind of silly formula with a billion other things in it--and read right off the side of the container that it will reduce your workout fatigue, and increase your workout capacity. If you take it home and use it, that's exactly what it will do. You'll experience less soreness, faster recovery, and better performance in the gym.

I'm not saying that I know what it takes to claim that the science here is false. I'm just saying that the guy that presented it in this article clearly doesn't get the picture well enough to communicate it clearly. And, if I'm being perfectly honest, even though I know I don't have the chops to say so declaratively, it's my opinion that the whole 'phosphate channel causes soreness' thing is BS.

“We are not one hundred per cent certain what causes muscles to become stiff during exercise,” says Jostein Hallén, a professor of physiology at the Norwegian School of Sport Sciences. “Our muscles may stiffen both at low concentrations of lactic acid and at high concentrations.”
